title: Electric circuits
ks3: Electricity and electromagnetism: current, potential difference, resistance, series and parallel circuits
intro: Cells, bulbs, switches and wires. Practise circuit symbols, current and voltage, series and parallel circuits, and resistance.
description: Free KS3 Physics electric circuits questions with answers: conductors and insulators, current and potential difference, ammeters and voltmeters, series and parallel circuits, and resistance. Marked instantly, for Year 7, 8 and 9 (ages 9 to 14).

questions.q: What does a cell (battery) do in a circuit?
options: It pushes the current round the circuit
questions.hint: Without it, nothing would flow.
questions.explain: A cell provides the push (the potential difference) that makes charge flow round the circuit, carrying energy to the components.

questions.q: The switch in this circuit is open. Does the bulb light?
options: No, because the circuit is not complete
questions.hint: Current can only flow round a complete loop.
questions.explain: An open switch makes a gap, so the circuit is not complete. No current flows and the bulb stays off.

questions.q: Which of these is a good electrical conductor?
questions.hint: Wires are made of it.
questions.explain: Metals like copper let current flow easily, so they are conductors. Plastic, rubber and wood are insulators.

questions.q: Why are electrical wires covered in plastic?
options: Plastic is an insulator, so it keeps us safe
It makes the wire stronger magnetically
questions.hint: Plastic does not let current flow through it.
questions.explain: Plastic is an insulator. It stops the current from flowing into anyone who touches the wire.

questions.q: There is a gap in a circuit between two wires. Which object would make the bulb light if you used it to bridge the gap?
questions.hint: The object must let current flow through it.
questions.explain: A paper clip is made of metal (steel), which is a conductor, so it completes the circuit. Rubber, plastic and wood are insulators.

questions.q: What is an electric current?
options: A flow of charge round a circuit
The push that the cell gives
How hard it is for charge to flow
questions.hint: Think of something moving all the way round the loop.
questions.explain: Current is a flow of charge. In metal wires the charges that move are electrons. The push is the potential difference, and how hard it is to flow is the resistance.

questions.q: How is current measured?
questions.hint: "Amp" is in the name of the meter.
questions.explain: Current is measured in amps (A) with an ammeter, connected in series.

questions.q: How is a voltmeter connected to measure the potential difference (voltage) across a bulb?
questions.hint: It compares the two sides of the bulb.
questions.explain: A voltmeter is connected across the component, in parallel with it, to measure the potential difference.

questions.q: What is the unit of resistance?
questions.hint: Its symbol is the Greek letter omega.
questions.explain: Resistance is measured in ohms (Ω).

questions.q: A cell is labelled **1.5 V**. What does the V stand for?
questions.hint: It is the unit of potential difference.
questions.explain: V stands for volts, the unit of potential difference (voltage). A 1.5 V cell gives a push of 1.5 volts.

questions.q: A torch has two 1.5 V cells in series, both facing the same way. What is their total potential difference?
questions.hint: When cells are joined in series the same way round, their pushes add up.

questions.q: Why must an ammeter be connected in series with a bulb, not across it?
options: So that the current through the bulb also flows through the ammeter
So that it can measure the voltage
So that it uses up less current
So that the bulb gets brighter
questions.hint: An ammeter counts the charge flowing through it.
questions.explain: An ammeter measures the current flowing through it. Putting it in series, in the same loop as the bulb, means the same current flows through both.

questions.q: The ammeter reads 0.2 A. What is the current through each bulb?
questions.hint: In a series circuit there is only one path.
questions.explain: In a series circuit the current is the same everywhere, so it is 0.2 A through each bulb.

questions.q: In a series circuit with three bulbs, one bulb breaks. What happens?
options: Only the broken bulb goes out
questions.hint: There is only one path for the current.
questions.explain: A broken bulb makes a gap in the only path, so the current stops and all the bulbs go out.

questions.q: More identical bulbs are added in series to the same cell. What happens to each bulb?
questions.hint: More bulbs in series means more resistance.
questions.explain: Adding bulbs in series increases the total resistance, so the current falls and each bulb is dimmer.

questions.q: How many paths can the current take in a series circuit?
questions.hint: "Series" means one thing after another, in a single loop.
questions.explain: A series circuit is a single loop, so there is only one path. The same current flows through every component.

questions.q: A 6 V battery is connected to two different bulbs in series. A voltmeter across the first bulb reads 4 V. What is the potential difference across the second bulb?
questions.hint: In a series circuit, the battery's potential difference is shared between the components.
questions.explain: The p.d. across the bulbs adds up to the battery's p.d.: 6 V − 4 V = 2 V.

questions.q: The main ammeter reads 0.6 A and the top branch reads 0.2 A. What does the bottom branch ammeter read?
questions.hint: The current splits between the branches, and the branch currents add up to the main current.
questions.explain: 0.6 A − 0.2 A = 0.4 A. (The two bulbs must be different, or the currents would be equal.)

questions.q: Each branch ammeter reads 0.1 A. What does the main ammeter (next to the cell) read?
questions.hint: Add up the currents in the branches.

questions.q: In a parallel circuit, one bulb breaks. What happens to the other bulbs?
questions.hint: Each bulb has its own path back to the cell.
questions.explain: In a parallel circuit each branch is its own loop, so the other bulbs stay on. That is why the lights in a house are wired in parallel.

questions.q: A 6 V battery is connected to two bulbs in parallel. What is the potential difference across each bulb?
questions.hint: Each branch is connected straight across the battery.
questions.explain: In a parallel circuit every branch gets the full potential difference of the battery, so each bulb has 6 V across it.

questions.q: The two bulbs are identical. The main ammeter reads 0.8 A. What does each branch ammeter read?
questions.hint: Identical bulbs share the current equally.
questions.explain: The branch currents add up to the main current. With identical bulbs it splits equally: 0.8 A ÷ 2 = 0.4 A in each branch.

questions.q: There is a potential difference of 6 V across a resistor and a current of 2 A through it. What is its resistance? (R = V ÷ I)
questions.hint: Divide the voltage by the current.

questions.q: A current of 4 A flows through a 3 Ω resistor. What is the potential difference across it? (V = I × R)
questions.hint: Multiply the current by the resistance.

questions.q: A long piece of thin wire is swapped for a shorter piece of the same wire. What happens to the resistance?
questions.hint: A longer wire is harder for the charge to get through.
questions.explain: The longer the wire, the bigger its resistance. A shorter piece of the same wire has less resistance, so more current flows.

questions.q: A 6 V battery is connected across a 30 Ω resistor. What current flows through it? (I = V ÷ R)
questions.hint: Divide the potential difference by the resistance.

questions.q: A resistor has a current of 0.5 A when the potential difference across it is 3 V. The p.d. is raised to 6 V and the resistance stays the same. What is the new current?
questions.hint: First find the resistance with R = V ÷ I.
questions.explain: R = 3 V ÷ 0.5 A = 6 Ω. Then I = V ÷ R = 6 V ÷ 6 Ω = 1 A. Doubling the p.d. doubles the current.
